title: Molecular detection of biofilm-related genes and antimicrobial resistance patterns in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from Northern Iran
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is widely recognized as one of the primary opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of nosocomial infections, notably in immunocompromised patients. Antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation, as two major virulence factors of P. aeruginosa, are related to the persistence of prolonged infections. This study was designed to (1) evaluate the frequency of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa in northern Iran and (2) analyze the frequency of biofilm-associated genes and their correlation with antimicrobial patterns. Clinical samples (n = 80) were collected from ICUs and other wards and processed for the isolation and identification of P. aeruginosa. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed using disk diffusion. PCR was performed to target the biofilm-associated genes. Out of 80 P. aeruginosa isolates, the prevalence of isolates was highest in the ICU (57.5%), and sputum was the most common specimen type (37%). Piperacillin/tazobactam demonstrated the highest activity (76.2% susceptible), followed by amikacin (52.5% susceptible). Notably, 45% of the isolates were MDR, 52.5% were XDR, while 2.5% were neither MDR nor XDR. The biofilm-associated genes ppyR and pslA were detected in 92.5% and 87.5% of the isolates, respectively, whereas pelA was found in 85% of the isolates. Among the 59 pelA, ppyR, and pslA-positive isolates, 47.45% were MDR, 42.37% were XDR, and 10.18% were non-MDR/XDR. Based on these outcomes, we strongly recommend strict infection prevention and control strategies to limit the transmission of MDR-PA, particularly in hospital settings. Piperacillin/tazobactam remains relatively effective; however, its administration should be guided by antimicrobial stewardship guidelines.

title: Catheter-related bloodstream infection reduction using systematic training in a Portuguese tertiary care hospital
abstract: Catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) are a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and increased healthcare costs among hospital-acquired infections. To reduce CRBSI, the Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance Program (UL-PPCIRA) reviewed current guidelines and implemented an intensive training project for healthcare professionals. Following the publication of care bundles, cascade training was conducted for staff involved in central line insertion and maintenance. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this continuous quality improvement project on CRBSI incidence in a tertiary hospital. Three consecutive periods of 2 years were analyzed: two before and one after implementation. CRBSI rates were 1.84, 1.68, and 0.65 per 1000 catheter-days in periods 1, 2, and 3, respectively. No significant difference was observed between periods 1 and 2 (IRR 0.92, 95% CI 0.52-1.63). In contrast, period 3 showed a significant reduction compared to period 2 (IRR 0.35, 95% CI 0.14-0.78;= .02). The implementation of standardized care bundles, supported by structured training, was associated with a significant reduction in CRBSI. Ongoing monitoring and reinforcement strategies are essential to ensure long-term sustainability.

title: Antibiotic-producing microorganisms: taxonomic diversity, screening strategies, and emerging and underexploited antibacterial targets
abstract: The discovery of antibiotics revolutionized modern medicine, but the escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) now severely compromises treatment efficacy. This review critically examines the diversity of antibiotic-producing microorganisms, with particular emphasis on strains isolated from extreme and underexplored ecological niches, and discusses how microbial interactions influence antibiotic biosynthesis. We summarize recent technological advances that have accelerated antibiotic discovery, including genome mining, innovative cultivation strategies, co-culture systems, and microfluidic platforms. Furthermore, we distinguish established antibacterial targets from emerging or noncanonical ones and evaluate them in terms of mechanistic validation, resistance liability, druggability, and translational relevance, encompassing cell wall precursor Lipid II, division protein FtsZ, epigenetic regulators, cytoskeletal MreB, peptidoglycan and Lipid A biosynthetic enzymes, DNA gyrase, topoisomerase IV, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, efflux pumps, and ATP synthase. We further discuss emerging antibacterial strategies, including multi-target mechanisms and resistance-informed target prioritization, as complementary approaches to limiting resistance evolution. Looking forward, we propose an integrated framework that unites three strategic priorities: harnessing untapped microbial resources, establishing high-efficiency screening pipelines, and advancing targeted biosynthetic engineering alongside validation of emerging and underexploited antibacterial targets. Within this framework, multi-target strategies are discussed as one potential approach to reduce resistance liability. Collectively, this integrated approach will facilitate a more focused R&D agenda, providing both a technical blueprint and strategic guidance for the development of next-generation antibiotics.

title: Selective electrochemical determination of norfloxacin in food samples using template-derived recognition cavities and conductive nanostructured networks
abstract: Norfloxacin (NFC) residues in food products remain a concern because of their potential contribution to antimicrobial resistance and adverse health effects. This study presents a disposable electrochemical method for the selective determination of NFC based on template-derived molecular recognition cavities integrated with a conductive AgNWs/MWCNTs nanostructured network on a screen-printed electrode. The conductive scaffold provided an enlarged electroactive surface and facilitated interfacial charge transfer, whereas the molecular recognition cavities enabled selective rebinding of NFC and improved discrimination against matrix interferences. The synergistic integration of molecular recognition and signal transduction generated a sensitive analytical interface for NFC determination in processed extracts from complex food matrices. Under optimized conditions, the proposed sensor exhibited a linear concentration range of 0.16-25.00 µM, with a detection limit of 0.04 µM. The analytical applicability of the method was evaluated using fortified processed extracts of milk, egg, and shrimp, yielding recoveries of 90.1-107.0%, 91.6-106.0%, and 91.7-106.0%, respectively, with relative standard deviations below 8.9%. A limited comparison with HPLC showed no statistically significant differences for the milk extracts at all investigated concentrations or for the egg and shrimp extracts at 25.0 µM; however, significant differences were observed at lower concentrations in the egg and shrimp extracts. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of molecular recognition cavity-based electrochemical sensing as a rapid, selective, and cost-effective strategy for screening NFC in processed food-sample extracts.

title: Stepwise evolution of tigecycline resistance in Enterococcus hirae through early IS1216E-mediated tet(L) amplification and subsequent rpsJ mutations
abstract: Enterococcus spp. from food animals represent important reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance; however, the mechanisms underlying tigecycline resistance remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the genetic basis and evolutionary dynamics of tigecycline resistance in Enterococcus hirae. Among 118 Enterococcus isolates recovered from 150 swine-derived samples, E. hirae was the predominant species (68/118, 57.63%). Tigecycline resistance was identified in ten isolates (10/118, 8.47%), all belonging to a single E. hirae clone. Whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate, EG2361, revealed three plasmids, among which pEG2361-2 harbored an IS1216E-associated multidrug resistance region capable of generating two circular translocatable units (TUs). TU1, carrying the promoter-variant tet(L) locus together with tet(M) and poxtA, underwent tandem amplification, leading to plasmid structural heterogeneity. Functional analyses demonstrated that tet(L) reduced tigecycline susceptibility, whereas enhanced resistance mainly associated with variation in the upstream promoter region rather than Tet(L) amino acid substitutions. Experimental evolution revealed a dynamic resistance trajectory. The initial increase in tigecycline resistance was associated with TU1 amplification and marked upregulation of tet(L) expression. Subsequently, tet(L) expression declined, whereas tigecycline minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) remained elevated and stable. Recurrent rpsJ mutations emerged independently across evolved lineages and were associated with high-level resistance. Together, these findings support a stepwise evolutionary model in which insertion sequence (IS)1216E-mediated amplification of the promoter-variant tet(L) locus drives rapid early adaptation, followed by the emergence of chromosomal rpsJ mutations associated with stable high-level resistance. This study expands current understanding of tigecycline resistance evolution in enterococci and highlights the interplay among mobile genetic elements, transcriptional regulation, and chromosomal adaptation in shaping antimicrobial resistance.

title: Mutation-Induced Conformational Remodeling of Dihydropteroate Synthase Governs Sulfonamide Resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major bacterial pathogen, and dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) is the primary target of sulfonamides (SAs). Environmental exposure to SAs promotes the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance. However, the molecular basis of DHPS mutation-mediated resistance remains unclear. Derived from the folP sequences of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-resistant clinical isolates, six clinically relevant DHPS mutants were constructed to investigate the molecular basis of resistance and to clarify how structure-activity relationships influence ligand recognition and binding modes. The results showed that the mutations altered the structural characteristics of the catalytic cavity and the substrate tunnel but exerted limited effects on the entry or binding of 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphate (DHPPP). DHPPP binding induced conformational remodeling, including expansion of loop 2 or loop 5 and rotation of HIE153. Compared with the wild type, sulfamethoxazole (SMX) exhibited reduced binding affinities across all mutants, with loop 2 expansion and impaired loop closure identified as the primary structural determinants of resistance. Additionally, HIE153 indirectly contributed to SMX recognition by maintaining the local microenvironment, binding pocket conformation, and neighboring interaction networks. Structure-activity relationship analysis showed that fused-ring sulfonamides exhibited the strongest tolerance to resistance-associated mutations. These findings reveal how DHPS mutations preserve natural-substrate recognition while selectively weakening SA binding, providing molecular-level insight into SA resistance and its implications for environmental antimicrobial resistance.

title: Substantial antibiotic resistance invasion of pristine river biofilms without specific alteration of the dominant community structure
abstract: The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) in freshwater ecosystems is increasingly recognized as a major environmental and public health concern. However, processes associated with the establishment of anthropogenic ARGs/MGEs in the environment remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the spatial dynamics of ARG/MGE entries along two low-impacted headwater rivers from pristine areas to the first signs of human activity. Epilithic biofilm and water samples collected along the river continuums during six sampling campaigns were analyzed using (i) high-throughput qPCR targeting a selection of 45 ARG and MGEs markers, (ii) microbial community dynamics by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, (iii) microbial source identification, and (iv) fecal coliforms enumeration. Both rivers exhibited a sharp increase in fecal contamination at the first inhabited areas, confirmed by human-specific microbial markers. This transition coincided with the abrupt introduction of anthropogenic ARGs/MGEs into river biofilms, whereas the relative abundance of these markers kept increasing further downstream. Notably, the widely used anthropogenic indicator intI1 exhibited an increasing relative abundance spanning five orders of magnitude starting from the pristine areas of the river, whereas ISEcp1, an insertion sequence involved in the mobilization of several ARGs, appeared immediately at the onset of anthropogenic influence. Although microbial community composition shifted markedly in one river, anthropogenic ARG/MGE invasion occurred with limited changes in community structure, indicating that resistance dissemination is not necessarily accompanied by detectable microbial replacement of the dominant community structure. Overall, these findings suggest that anthropogenic resistance determinants can establish within river biofilms even when the dominant microbial community remains largely unchanged.

title: Global phylogeography, genomic characteristics and transmission of antibiotic resistance of multi-drug resistant ORN-1-producing Raoultella ornithinolytica B1645-1B
abstract: To characterize the genomic phylogeny and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genotypes of the ORN-1-producing R. ornithinolytica B16451B, and to elucidate the transfer mechanisms of resistance genes at the genomic level. The genome of R. ornithinolytica B16451B was sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq 4000 and PacBio RSII sequencing platforms. A global phylogenetic analysis of the genomic data was conducted by the Center for Genomic Epidemiology (CGE), incorporating information on geographical distribution, isolation sources, and host associations. A comparative phylogenomic analysis was performed using the BLAST Ring Image Generator (BRIG). Genome annotation was performed using Glimmer and the Rapid Annotation using Subsystem Technology (RAST) server. Mobile genetic elements were predicted using TnCentral, ISFinder, and PHASTER. The antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) were analyzed using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), while the virulence factors genes (VFGs) were analyzed using the Virulence Factor Database (VFDB). Gene transfer experiments were conducted in the intestinal tract of mice. Transconjugants were identified using 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing, and drug-resistance genes were amplified by PCR. A chromosome (designated chromosome 01) was first identified in strain B16451B. A carrying IS4 insertion sequence distinct resistance region within this chromosome, designated B1645-1B-RG, harbors the β-lactamase gene bla. Three intact prophages, designated prophage YC1, YC2, and YC3, were also first identified. The blagene was successfully transferred from strain B16451B to Escherichia coli (designated B1645-1BLMY1) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (designated B1645-1BYCF2) in the intestines of mice. The strain B16451B harbored 25 antimicrobial resistance genes and 8 classes of virulence factor genes. Based on comparative genomic analysis of strains retrieved from the NCBI Genome Database, 98 antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) (e.g., sul1, bla, bla) among 234 R. ornithinolytica strains were identified to exhibit significantly higher prevalence in human isolates than in non-human host sources (e.g., water, animals, plants). The chromosome 01 was identified in a multi-drug resistant ORN-1-producing the strain B16451B isolated from China. The genome of strain B16451B harbors three integrated prophages: YC1 (42.2 kb), YC2 (60.5 kb), and YC3 (23.8 kb) was identified. The IS4 insertion might promote blagene transfer within the intestinal flora of mice. Among these 234 R. ornithinolytica strains analyzed in this study, most virulence factor genes (e.g., ompa, yagx/ecpc) and resistance genes (e.g., bla, bla) exhibited higher prevalence in Homo sapiens isolates than in strains from non-human sources including water, animals and plants. These findings provide valuable references for clinicians optimize the management of R. ornithinolytica infections and guide clinical treatment.

title: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?
abstract: Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own. Should concerns for future health be confined to the 21st century as per the stated mission of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health? If not, how far into the future should they extend, and why? Population ethics is a branch of ethics that considers future populations' wellbeing. This Review, a part of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health, applies general insights from population ethics to future populations' health, and shows why that application is more complex than meets the eye.

title: ERMA: a harmonizing epicPCR data analysis tool
abstract: EpicPCR links functional genes to taxonomic markers at the single-cell level and has become an important method in microbial ecology and antimicrobial resistance research. However, the lack of missing standardized data analysis workflows limits reproducibility and comparability across studies. Existing analyses are often based on custom, unpublished scripts, complicating cross-study benchmarking and reuse. We present ERMA, an open-source, Snakemake-based pipeline that enables an automated, standardized, reproducible, and scalable epicPCR data analysis with minimal user input. ERMA supports both Illumina and ONT sequencing data and integrates quality control, database preparation, dual similarity searches against taxonomic and functional reference databases, results integration, filtering, and visualization. The pipeline is adaptable to a broad range of research questions beyond AMR due to modular database preparation and integration of specific UniRef queries. We evaluated ERMA using five publicly available epicPCR datasets covering diverse sample sources and sequencing depths. Across these datasets, ERMA achieved mean concordance rates of approximately 70-83% with the taxonomic results reported in the respective publications. In addition, validation using a defined five-member mock community spiked into clinical wastewater demonstrated full recovery of mock genera, with 85% of ERMA-detected genera also detected by independent 16S rDNA gene analysis of the same wastewater sample. Attrition analysis showed inconsistent filtering patterns across studies, reflecting dataset-specific quality differences. While large-scale reference datasets for epicPCR remain limited, validation using both publicly available studies and a defined mock community shows strong, interpretable performance across heterogeneous datasets. By providing a transparent, modular, and reproducible workflow, ERMA contributes toward harmonized epicPCR data analysis and establishes a foundation for future methodological standardization and benchmarking efforts as reference datasets improve.

title: Mycoplasma genitalium prevalence, bacterial load, and antibiotic resistance in paired vaginal and anal specimens from Chlamydia trachomatis-infected women
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) frequently co-infects women with Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), but the epidemiology and clinical significance of this association remain poorly understood. This study assessed MG positivity, antimicrobial resistance, mgpB genotyping and bacterial load in paired self-collected vaginal and anal swabs from 426 women with urogenital CT infection, and assessed the risk factors for CT/MG coinfection compared with CT monoinfection. MG detection and quantification were carried out using an in-house quantitative PCR targeting the MgPa adhesin gene. Macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance-associated mutations were determined by sequencing the 23S RNA gene and the parC gene, respectively. The mgpB types were determined by sequencing a 281-bp region of the mgpB gene. Clinical, demographic, and behavioural characteristics were compared between women with CT monoinfection and CT/MG coinfection. MG was detected in 22.8% of women, more frequently in vaginal than anal specimens (18.5% vs 12.9%, p = 0.03). Among MG-positive women, 43.3% had vaginal-only infection, 18.6% anal-only infection, and 38.1% infection at both sites. Macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance were detected in 16.7% and 9.1% of evaluable cases, respectively. Anal MG was usually asymptomatic and unrelated to reported anal intercourse. MG bacterial load was significantly higher in vaginal than anal samples, and paired specimens shared identical mgpB genotypes, supporting the hypothesis of secondary anal colonization from the vagina. Being born in France was the only factor associated with CT/MG coinfection, compared with CT monoinfection in the multivariate analysis. MG coinfection did not influence the CT bacterial load. MG coinfection was common among women with CT infection but was not associated with higher CT bacterial load, more severe clinical manifestations, or distinct behavioural characteristics. Further studies are warranted to clarify the biological interactions between these two pathogens in women.

title: Large language model-assisted curation and sequence-informed modelling reveal membrane and genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance gene removal
abstract: Water acts as a critical medium for the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pose threats to public health. Efficient removal of extracellular ARGs (eARGs, hereafter ARGs) by functional membranes is critical for water security, yet their physicochemical heterogeneity poses significant challenges for membrane design. Herein, this study reports a large language model-driven machine learning framework to guide rational design of membranes with high selectivity for ARG removal. A large language model-based workflow was established to automatically extract standardized membrane and ARG datasets, followed by the development of a sequence-informed hierarchical filtration (SIHF) model for facilitating membrane design. By integrating sequence motif analysis of ARGs with membrane properties within a machine learning architecture, SIHF can identify the dominant factors governing ARG retention and quantify sequence-dependent incremental effects. SIHF analysis reveals that membrane pore size emerges as the primary design factor, with hydraulic flux modulating its impact. Independent filtration experiments further supported the predictive performance of SIHF. Overall, this work establishes an actionable and evidence-based design framework to advance the development of next generation membranes for controlling ARG dissemination and mitigating antimicrobial resistance.

title: Stage-wise far-UVC/chlorine process curbs antimicrobial resistance in hospital wastewater: Short-burst inactivation and sustained suppression of recovery and resistance transfer
abstract: Conventional UV/chlorine can leave incomplete genetic damage and create a low-dose window that promotes horizontal gene transfer (HGT), limiting reliable antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) control. Here, UV/chlorine (1 mg/L free chlorine) was evaluated in 0.22-μm-filtered hospital wastewater inoculated with E. coli DH5α-RP4 and compared with UV, UV, and UV/chlorine. During UV/chlorine treatment in hospital wastewater, free available chlorine (FAC) declined rapidly and approached the detection limit at approximately 35 mJ/cm, whereas UV/chlorine retained measurable FAC at 100 mJ/cm. Chloride promoted conversion of Cl· to selective Cl·, whereas tert-butanol quenching indicated a smaller contribution from ·OH. Accordingly, the process comprised an initial chlorine-enhanced phase (0-35 mJ/cm), which delivered ∼2.5-log greater ARB inactivation than UValone, followed by a UV-dominated phase after FAC depletion. Membrane permeabilization largely saturated during Stage 1, supporting an acute rather than dose-proportional envelope attack. At 100 mJ/cm, UV/chlorine prevented regrowth, reduced intracellular antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) by 76.6-88.3%, and drove RP4 conjugation toward zero. In contrast, UV/chlorine transiently increased conjugation to ∼150% of the control at low doses. Transcriptomics showed concurrent suppression of envelope maintenance, DNA repair, protein homeostasis, and metabolism. Thus, UV/chlorine combines a short RCS shock with sustained multi-target damage to control ARB, ARG persistence, and plasmid-mediated HGT in complex wastewater.

title: Combination-specific effects of antibiotic and disinfectant co-contamination on the enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes in sediments
abstract: The environmental co-occurrence of disinfectants and antibiotics has emerged as a typical multi-pollutant issue, with river sediments serving as critical sinks and accumulation media. However, whether their combined exposure accelerate antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) dissemination in sediments remains unclear. Here, we systematically evaluated the effects of single and combined exposures to sodium hypochlorite and representative antibiotics on the sediment resistome and microbial communities. The results demonstrated that combined exposure generally increased the relative abundances of ARGs (1.83- to 3.57-fold) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs, 2.39- to 22.28-fold). Notably, sodium hypochlorite-gentamicin combination exhibited the most pronounced synergistic effect, consistent with toxicological model prediction. Combined exposure also reshaped bacterial community structure and enriched potential ARG-host taxa, while co-occurrence network analysis identified Limosilactobacillus as a candidate genus associated with multiple ARGs. Mechanistically, partial least squares path modeling indicated that MGE-mediated horizontal gene transfer was the dominant pathway driving ARGs enrichment. Plasmid conjugation assays further showed that NaClO + gentamicin increased conjugation frequency by 3.81-fold, supporting enhanced horizontal gene transfer. Overall, this study elucidates the intrinsic mechanisms by which complex pollution drives ARGs propagation in sediments, highlighting the overlooked ecological risks associated with disinfectant-antibiotic co-contamination in aquatic environments.

title: In vitro activity and comparative efficacy of novel nitrofuran-containing ciprofloxacin analogs against bacterial pathogens including ciprofloxacin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: The rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance, especially in Staphylococcus aureus, highlights the urgent need for improved antibacterial agents. In 2019 alone, AMR caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths and contributed to nearly 5 million more globally. Here, we present the design, synthesis, and testing of modified ciprofloxacin analogs bearing nitrofuran, furan, and spirocyclic diamine moieties. Among these compounds, two showed a more than eight-fold increase in potency against ciprofloxacin-resistant S.aureus ISR14-002 compared to ciprofloxacin, demonstrating improved activity against a ciprofloxacin-resistant strain. In vivo testing using a Galleria mellonella infection model with S. aureus SG511 demonstrated that compound 12 conferred a survival benefit comparable to ciprofloxacin. Improved activity was most notable against Gram-positive bacteria, especially our target pathogen S. aureus. However, the spectrum of organism selectivity varied by analog, highlighting the effects of focused structural modification. These results suggest that the fluoroquinolone scaffold can be modified to circumvent ciprofloxacin resistance and expand its spectrum of activity, while retaining acceptable cellular toxicity.

title: Population size modulates the transition from gene amplification-mediated heteroresistance to stable resistance
abstract: Heteroresistance is characterized by antibiotic-resistant subpopulations which can be underpinned by reversible gene duplication-amplification (GDA) of antibiotic resistance genes. It is often considered a precursor of stable resistance mutations. We investigated the evolutionary dynamics between GDA-mediated heteroresistance and stable resistance mutations in a clinical Enterobacter cloacae complex isolate. Exposure to ceftazidime resulted in enrichment of ampC β-lactamase GDAs in a concentration-dependent manner. Long-term exposure and high concentrations of ceftazidime selected for stable resistance mutations in dacB and ampD, a decrease of GDAs and a loss of population heterogeneity. Evolution experiments and mathematical modelling suggest that, in large populations, competition with GDA-carrying subpopulations can prolong fixation of stable resistance mutations in the population. By contrast, heteroresistance rescues small populations upon sudden antibiotic challenge, thereby acting as a precursor of stable resistance. This study highlights a previously underappreciated dual, population-size dependent role for GDAs in the transition from heteroresistance to stable resistance.

title: Economic evaluation of antimicrobial stewardship programme in primary care in Kosovo: study protocol
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a major challenge to both public health and economic stability in many countries. In response, antimicrobial stewardship programmes are essential for optimising antibiotic use and reducing antimicrobial resistance, particularly in primary care settings where most antibiotics are prescribed. Kosovo, like many countries, is increasingly affected by the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance and must strengthen its strategies to address this problem. Although national action plans on antimicrobial resistance and stewardship have been completed, there is limited evidence on the economic impact of antimicrobial stewardship interventions in Kosovo, as is the case in many low- and middle-income country contexts. This study thus aims to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of antimicrobial stewardship programme in Kosovo, and the cost of implementing this programme in primary care settings in Kosovo. First, for the cost-effectiveness component of the study, we will use a quasi-experimental interrupted time series design focusing on patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with upper respiratory tract infections at intervention and control sites in Kosovo’s primary care system, to analyse changes in antibiotic consumption measured in defined daily doses, and estimate the corresponding monetary value to determine cost-effectiveness. Second, we will use a bottom-up costing method to estimate the costs associated with implementing the antimicrobial stewardship programme, including resources required across intervention and control sites. Cost data for both components will be collected from the implementing institutions and the main family medicine centres, serving as the intervention and control sites. The Ethical Committee of the Kosovo Chamber of Medical Doctors approved the protocol of our study (Number: 122/2024). Moreover, the results from this study will be published and disseminated as a peer-reviewed publication.

title: Development of an Intein-Based Bioprocessing Platform for Recombinant Production of a Potent Antimicrobial Peptide: Lasioglossin-III
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the demand for novel anti-infective agents, positioning antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) as promising therapeutic alternatives. However, large scale production of AMPs remains challenging due to their small size, cationic nature, host toxicity, and high cost of chemical synthesis. In this study, we report an efficient and economically viable intein-mediated recombinant bioprocess for the production of the short antimicrobial peptide Lasioglossin-III (LL-III) in its C-terminally amidated form using Escherichia coli-based expression platform. A codon-optimized LL-III gene was fused to the Mxe GyrA intein along with a chitin binding domain (CBD) using the pTWIN1 expression system, enabling stable expression, affinity purification, and controlled auto-cleavage. The fusion protein was expressed in soluble form at low temperature and purified using chitin resin under optimized binding conditions. Notably, the chitin resin retained its binding capacity across multiple reuse cycles, improving the overall process-economics; auto-cleavage under mild reducing conditions released the mature peptide, which was confirmed by RP-HPLC and LC/MS to be identical to chemically synthesized standard peptide. The optimized process yielded ∼4.4 mg Lof recombinant peptide leading to significant reduction in production costs at the current cleavage efficiency. Overall, this study establishes a scalable, environmentally sustainable, and cost-effective bioprocessing platform not only for short AMPs, but also for other peptide-based therapeutics as well.

title: Farming systems shape distinct ARGs removal pathways: Biotic-driven in large-scale composting versus abiotic-driven in free-range systems
abstract: Current research on antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) removal during manure composting has primarily focused on differences across animal species. However, how farming practices, which fundamentally differ in feed composition, antibiotic use, and rearing density, shape ARGs removal patterns and underlying mechanisms remains poorly understood. Here we compared manure composting between large-scale (LS) and free-range (FR) systems and revealed fundamentally divergent causal pathways governing ARGs dynamics. LS achieved higher removal rates of total ARGs (93% vs 57%) and total mobile genetic elements (MGEs; 93% vs 77%) than FR, operating through a biotic-driven mechanism: composting conditions suppressed specialized bacterial consortia that served as primary ARGs hosts, with biotic factors exerting a dominant effect on ARGs variation (path coefficient: r = 0.92). In contrast, FR relied on an abiotic-factor-dominated dual-suppression mechanism, with the abiotic latent variable exerting a dominant negative effect on ARGs abundance (r = -0.59), while biotic contributions were minimal (r = 0.26). Driven by their distinct feed origins, key nutritional components diverged significantly between systems: nitrogen-related factors [total nitrogen (TN) + protein (P)] dominated ARGs variation in LS (56.86%), whereas TS was the predominant driver in FR (76.06%). FR also exhibited greater microbial richness and a wider variety of genera, but lacked specialized ARG-hosting consortia, explaining its lower removal efficiency. Collectively, our findings reveal system-associated differences in the mechanistic pathways of ARGs removal between the two farming systems, underscoring the potential necessity for system-specific composting strategies.

title: Comprehensive Characterization of Bioaerosol Microbial Communities, ARG, and Occupational Exposure Risks in WWTP and Comprehensive Landfill
abstract: In the sewage treatment plant and landfill in the same area, the differences in transmission characteristics of potential pathogenic microorganisms and antibiotic resistance genes/movable genetic elements (ARGs/MGEs) mediated by bioaerosols have not been fully studied. Therefore, we integrated 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, high-throughput quantitative PCR, quantitative microbial risk assessment, exposure-dose estimation, and machine learning to compare microbial communities, antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements (ARGs/MGEs), and estimated occupational exposure levels at a wastewater treatment plant (XQ) and an integrated solid waste treatment facility (DP) in Central China. The mean culturable bacterial concentration was 3.4-fold higher at DP than at XQ (1726 CFU/m, 502 CFU/m), and proportion of fine biogenic particles was also higher at DP (27%, 15%). In contrast, mean airborne concentration of ARGs/MGEs was substantially higher at XQ than at DP (5462 copies/m, 584 copies/m), resulting in a higher estimated inhalation exposure dose at XQ. The dominant resistance determinants were ermC, dhps, and intI1 at XQ, and cmxA, tnpA-05, and lnuA-01 at DP. Machine learning analysis identified Faecalibacterium as an important microbial feature distinguishing solid waste bioaerosols, whereas blaPAO was among most influential ARG features associated with XQ bioaerosols. Partial least squares regression revealed extensive covariation between bacterial genera and resistance determinants. Achromobacter was positively associated with ermX at XQ and with intI1 at DP, although these associations do not establish direct host-gene relationships. Overall, two facilities showed contrasting bioaerosol exposure profiles, characterized by higher bacterial and fine-particle levels at DP and higher ARG/MGE exposure estimates at XQ. These findings support facility-specific occupational aerosol control and monitoring strategies.

title: Understanding the complexity of microplastics, antibiotic resistance, and their interaction with human health and ecosystems: a review towards global environmental sustainability
abstract: Microplastics (MPs), defined as particles with a diameter <5 mm, are increasingly recognized as important global environmental stressors due to their ubiquity and harmful effects on organisms. Although most studies have investigated the direct biological effects of MPs, their role in the spread of pathogens and antibiotic resistance remains less explored. Thanks to their hydrophobic surfaces, MPs act as substrates for microbial colonization, giving rise to the plastisphere-a microenvironment that hosts opportunistic and clinically relevant bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Vibrio spp., and Aeromonas spp., some of which are multidrug-resistant. The plastisphere has emerged as a hotspot for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), promoting horizontal gene transfer (HGT) and contributing to the environmental spread of resistance. Human exposure to MPs is widespread, as have been detected in water, food, and air. Once ingested or inhaled, they can accumulate in tissues, cross biological barriers, and cause gastrointestinal irritation, dysbiosis of the microbiota, endocrine disruptions, oxidative stress, and immunotoxicity. MPs carrying biofilms containing resistant bacteria and ARGs represent a direct route of exposure for the introduction of resistance factors into the human body, increasing the risk of untreatable infections. Despite growing evidence, significant knowledge gaps remain regarding the role of MPs in the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and associated health risks. To date, no legislation specifically considers MPs as vectors of pathogens and ARGs. This review aims to clarify the concept of the plastisphere, its implications for AMR, and the urgent need for interdisciplinary approaches to address this emerging global threat.

title: Role of the urobiome in urinary tract infections: current knowledge and research prospects
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly cystitis, are among the most common bacterial infections worldwide, with a disproportionate burden on adult female individuals, who often have recurrence. The discovery of the urobiome, a low microbial biomass community in the urinary tract, has transformed our understanding of UTI pathogenesis and infection susceptibility. Experimental and omics approaches provide insights into the taxonomic and functional complexity of the urobiome, highlighting the importance of microbial metabolites, ecological interactions, and host-microbe dynamics. Polymicrobial interactions within the urobiome further modulate pathogenicity, with some microbes inhibiting or promoting uropathobionts. Advancing UTI management will require combining omics and experimental research with ecological and evolutionary insights. This approach can enable the development of personalised, non-antibiotic interventions, such as live biotherapeutics and prebiotics, to improve diagnostics, reduce antibiotic resistance, and enhance treatment efficacy.

title: Enhancing humification enzymatic activity and antibiotic resistance gene attenuation in aerobic composting of sewage sludge and food waste: The role of calcium oxide amendment
abstract: Organic municipal solid waste (OMSW) management remains a global challenge, intensifying with rapid urbanization and the widespread use of antibiotics for various purposes. These practices contribute to the dissemination of emerging contaminants, particularly antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Composting is widely applied for OMSW treatment, however the effectiveness of calcium oxide (CaO) amendment in mitigating ARGs and enhancing humification remains limited. This research investigated the effects of CaO amendment at varying levels (T1-0.25 %, T2-0.5 %, and T3-1 % w/w) on humification, enzymatic activities, microbial community succession, changes in dissolved organic matter (DOM), and ARG attenuation during aerobic composting. The results show that T3 (1 % CaO) achieved the highest humic acid formation (51.07 g/kg) and ARG reduction (2.3 log). However, T2 (0.5 % CaO) provided the most favorable overall balance across the evaluated parameters, including compost maturity, microbial community diversity, enzymatic activity, and ARG attenuation, without the inhibitory effects associated with excessive alkalinity. The initial ARG abundance was 2.82 × 10copies/g dry weight (dw) compost, ARG-subtypes aadD, aac(6')-lb-01, mefA, and sul1 were the pre-dominated subtypes ranging 1.42 × 10 - 2.74 × 10copies/g dry dw compost significantly reduced by 2.3 log in T3 and 2.1 log in T1 compared to CK trial (0.88 log). Microbial study indicated a rapid succession towards communities dominated by Actinobacteria and Chloroflexi at moderate CaO concentrations. These results demonstrate that CaO regulates composting through several physicochemical and microbial mechanisms, offering a promising strategy to enhance compost maturity and environmental safety.

title: Community-acquired Acinetobacter baumannii pneumonia in Southern Vietnam: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii has traditionally been considered a nosocomial pathogen, but cases of community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia have increasingly been reported in tropical Asia, including Vietnam. Data on its clinical characteristics, antimicrobial resistance, and patient outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to describe the clinical profile, resistance patterns, and outcomes of community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia in southern Vietnam. We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study at Nhan Dan Gia Dinh Hospital, a 1500-bed tertiary center in Ho Chi Minh City (January 2021-December 2023). Adults (≥18 years) with community-acquired pneumonia and a positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or blood culture for A. baumannii obtained within 48 hours of admission were included. Patients with cultures >48 hours after admission, hospitalization in the prior 90 days, residence in/transfer from another facility ≥48 hours preadmission, polymicrobial cultures, or incomplete records were excluded. Thirty-one patients were identified (median age 69.0 years (interquartile range 64.0-84.0); 83.9% male; 83.9% current/former smokers). No clear seasonal predominance was observed within the study window after month-level normalization. On admission, 87.1% had hypoxemia (peripheral oxygen saturation<90%) and nearly half (45.2%) were severe community-acquired pneumonia. Antibiotic escalation was required in 61.3% after a median of 4 days (interquartile range 3-5). Resistance was approximately 69%-83% across the routinely tested β-lactams and fluoroquinolones, whereas aminoglycosides showed comparatively higher in vitro activity than the other tested antibiotic classes but susceptibility remained suboptimal (amikacin 50%, tobramycin 46%, gentamicin 36%). Initial empiric therapy was active against the index isolate in 4/25 patients (16.0%) with available susceptibility results. In-hospital mortality was 13/31 (41.9%). Community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia is associated with severe disease, extensive antimicrobial resistance, frequent empiric treatment mismatch, and high mortality. In resource-constrained settings, limited therapeutic options highlight the importance of early microbiological diagnosis, comprehensive susceptibility testing, and locally informed treatment strategies.

title: Phage-ICE tandems facilitate bacterial adaptation and antimicrobial resistance spread
abstract: Phages and integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) drive bacterial evolution, but how their interplay shapes bacterial adaptation and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dissemination remains unclear. Here, we characterize phage-ICE tandems formed by site-specific accretion of phages and ICEs into cotransferable units. In, phage-encoded integrases (IntIE) drive stress-inducible excision and circularization, after which ICE machinery mediates conduction of the tandem. When excision is impaired, phage and phage-ICE fragments disseminate by transformation and integrate via RecA-dependent homologous recombination (HR), providing a fail-safe route. This pathway enables cotransfer of flanking chromosomal DNA, generating length-variable integrations that remodel transcriptional programs and increase oxidative stress tolerance. A global screen identified 612 phage-ICE tandems across seven phyla and 135 species, including multidrug-resistant pathogens, with lineage-specific repertoires of AMR, virulence, and metabolic genes. Rather than a hybrid element, these structures represent functional interplay where prophages exploit ICE conjugation while facilitating mobilization of the composite region. By coupling excision, transfer, and recombination, phage-ICEs shape adaptation and accelerate AMR spread.

title: Machine learning for estimating and comparing clinical rules for treating diarrheal illness with antibiotics
abstract: Acute diarrheal disease is a leading cause of death in children under age 5, disproportionately impacting children in low-resource settings. Although many cases could respond to antibiotic treatment, the benefits of widely prescribing antibiotics must be weighed against the risks of antimicrobial resistance. These challenges motivate development of individualized treatment guidelines for diarrheal disease. In this study, we utilize a framework for creation and evaluation of individualized treatment rules that leverage diagnostic and clinical information to make treatment recommendations. In contrast to many applications of pipelines for creating and evaluating treatment rules, we (i) explicitly create rules that limit the proportion of children treated based on expected clinical benefit, to limit risks for overtreatment and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, and (ii) propose methods to compare rules based on different sets of input covariates, allowing for quantification of the impact of measuring additional biomarkers in clinical settings. We use a nested cross-validation procedure with ensemble machine learning and doubly-robust estimation to derive, evaluate, and compare rules. We demonstrate that our proposed method yields appropriate inference in a realistic simulation study and apply our method to data from the AntiBiotics for Children with severe Diarrhea (ABCD) trial.

title: Gram-Positive Bacteria Responses to Antibiotics When Incubated in Fecal in Vitro Microcosms from Swine Supplemented with Chlorophyllin
abstract: Standardized antimicrobial susceptibility assays use defined culture media and may therefore not fully account for gastrointestinal constituents that influence bacterial responses to antibiotics. This study evaluated whether swine fecal extracts, including extracts associated with dietary chlorophyllin supplementation, altered the antimicrobial susceptibility of multidrug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria. Fecal material collected from pigs fed either a non-chlorophyllin or chlorophyllin-supplemented diet was pooled by dietary group, processed to produce clarified fecal extracts, and incorporated at 20% (vol/vol) into Mueller-Hinton (MH) broth. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of chlortetracycline, penicillin, carbadox, tylosin, ceftazidime, and norfloxacin were determined for selected,, andstrains using broth microdilution and compared with MICs obtained in standard MH broth. Fecal extracts altered MICs in a strain- and antibiotic-dependent manner. Extracts from chlorophyllin-fed pigs produced particularly pronounced reductions in susceptibility thresholds for several combinations, including >128- to >256-fold decreases in chlortetracycline MICs for,, andH 1019 V; >253-fold decreases in penicillin MICs for several strains; and >32- to >256-fold decreases in ceftazidime MICs for four strains. Carbadox MICs were also reduced in several organisms. However, these effects were not universal: tylosin MICs were generally unchanged or increased, and norfloxacin MICs were unchanged or increased in all strains tested. Fecal extracts from non-chlorophyllin-fed pigs also altered MICs, demonstrating that the fecal matrix itself influenced phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility. These findings indicate that antimicrobial susceptibility measured under standard laboratory conditions may differ substantially in the presence of fecal-derived constituents and support further characterization of the metabolites responsible for these effects.

title: Characterization of a K62-specific phage depolymerase and its protective effect in a mouse model of Klebsiella pneumoniae infection
abstract: Multidrug-resistantKlebsiella pneumoniae has emerged as a formidable healthcare challenge, driving the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies such as phage therapy. In this study, we isolated and comprehensively characterized a novel phage, designated vB_Kp_IME328 (IME328), which exhibits highly specific bactericidal activity against K62-type K. pneumoniae. Morphological analyses revealed that IME328 forms plaques surrounded by distinct translucent halos and possesses a long tail, clustering it within the Webervirus genus. Through whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatic analysis, we identified ORF3 as the gene encoding a putative tail-fiber depolymerase. This gene was successfully cloned and expressed, yielding the recombinant protein Dp3. Functional assays confirmed that Dp3 possesses robust depolymerizing and antibacterial activities. In vitro, Dp3 acted synergistically with serum to effectively eradicate the target bacteria. Furthermore, live/dead cell staining and cellular assays demonstrated that Dp3 significantly enhances the phagocytic and intracellular bactericidal capacities of macrophages. In vivo evaluations using a lethal murine bacteremia model (inoculated with 6 × 10⁷ CFU) showed that Dp3 administration conferred 100% protection and survival, whereas all untreated infected mice succumbed to the infection. Together, our findings highlight the targeted anti-virulence properties of the depolymerase Dp3. By enhancing host-mediated immune clearance, Dp3 offers a promising therapeutic strategy against antibiotic-resistant K62-type K. pneumoniae infections.

title: Integrated morpho-biochemical, molecular, phylogenetic, and thermodynamic characterization of Bacillus isolates from ecologically distinct Indian soils
abstract: Soil microorganisms represent an invaluable reservoir of taxonomic diversity and functional traits with immense potential for sustainable agriculture, environmental management, and microbial biotechnology. In the present study, eight bacterial isolates were characterized from soils collected from three ecologically distinct regions of India. Comprehensive morpho-biochemical characterization revealed that all representative isolates (AMU-UP-1, AMU-K-1, and AMU-MY-1) were Gram-positive, catalase-positive, and Voges-Proskauer-positive, whereas the Methyl Red test differentiated isolate AMU-K-1 from AMU-UP-1 and AMU-MY-1, indicating metabolic heterogeneity. Antimicrobial susceptibility analysis demonstrated clear inhibition zones against tetracycline, amoxicillin, and azithromycin in agar well diffusion assays; however, broth microdilution assays revealed substantial variability in antibiotic resistance. Molecular characterization generated high-quality ~1500 bp 16S rRNA amplicons, producing sequencing reads of 1,048 bp (AMU-K-1) and 1,102 bp (AMU-UP-1). BLAST analysis identified AMU-K-1 as closely related to Bacillus safensis (GenBank: PZ619164), whereas AMU-UP-1 exhibited 100% sequence identity to multiple closely related taxa within the Bacillus subtilis/ Bacillus velezensis species complex (GenBank: PZ619172), precluding unambiguous species-level resolution based on 16S rRNA gene data alone. Phylogenetic reconstruction using the Tamura 3-parameter model with invariant sites (T92+I) confirmed their evolutionary placement within well-supported Bacillus lineages, while nucleotide substitution analysis demonstrated a pronounced transition bias over transversions across more than 1,300 aligned nucleotide positions. Computational RNA secondary structure prediction further revealed highly stable ribosomal conformations, with minimum free energies of -530.80 kcal mol⁻for AMU-K-1 and -523.80 kcal mol⁻for AMU-UP-1. Notably, AMU-K-1 exhibited greater in silico ensemble diversity (357.82) than AMU-UP-1 (151.53), suggesting differences in predicted conformational flexibility; however these computational properties translate to physiological adaptability require direct experimental verification. The integration of phenotypic, biochemical, molecular, phylogenetic, antimicrobial, and thermodynamic analyses provides a comprehensive characterization of indigenous Bacillus isolates and establishes a valuable resource for future exploitation in plant growth promotion, biological control, environmental bioremediation, and microbial biotechnology.

title: Assessment of pathogenic traits in selected bacteria isolated from snowy environments in France and Greenland
abstract: Microorganisms inhabiting cold environments have gained increasing attention in recent decades due to their unique adaptation mechanisms that enable survival under extreme conditions. Growing evidence indicates that some cold-adapted bacteria possess phenotypic and genomic traits linked to pathogenicity, raising concerns about their potential environmental and public health relevance. Here, we characterized three culturable bacteria isolated from human-impacted snow in the French Alps (Chamrousse) and coastal Greenland (Nuuk). Snow samples were cultured on R2A medium, and isolates were identified by Sanger sequencing as Peribacillus, Sphingomonas, and Subtercola. Temperature tolerance, haemolytic activity, and antibiotic susceptibility were assessed by culture-based assays, while whole-genome sequencing was used to screen for antibiotic resistance and virulence-associated genes using reference databases. Only the Peribacillus isolate tolerated 37 °C and showed α-haemolysis. Antibiotic susceptibility testing indicated full susceptibility in Peribacillus, while Sphingomonas and Subtercola showed reduced susceptibility to a limited number of antibiotics, mainly to cefotaxime, chloramphenicol, and colistin. Genomes encoded genes associated with efflux, target modification, motility/adhesion, and stress adaptation, indicating environmental resilience rather than clinical pathogenicity. Overall, these isolates displayed limited pathogenic phenotypes with genomic traits primarily supporting environmental adaptation and survival.

title: Escherichia coli bacteriophage vB_EcoS_MS2 effectively prevents biofilm formation but shows limited activity against mature biofilms
abstract: Pathogenic Escherichia coli biofilms pose a significant challenge in veterinary and clinical settings due to their high antibiotic resistance. This study characterizes the E. coli bacteriophage vB_EcoS_MS2 as a potential targeted biocontrol agent against these pathogens. Host range determination revealed high specificity, with vB_EcoS_MS2 lysing only select E. coli strains and demonstrating superior replication efficiency (Efficiency of Plating: 112.57%) on strain C4 compared to its propagation host, MS2. While nutrient limitation strongly induced biofilm formation in in vitro assays, phage vB_EcoS_MS2 demonstrated potent prophylactic activity, inhibiting initial biofilm development by over 70% across all tested concentrations (10⁴-10⁹ PFU/mL). Conversely, the phage showed limited and transient efficacy in eradicating mature, 48-hour-old biofilms under the tested conditions. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed a 40,209 bp circular genome belonging to the class Caudoviricetes, encoding a robust holin-endopeptidase lytic cassette without carrying known antimicrobial resistance determinants. These findings indicate that while vB_EcoS_MS2 is highly effective for prophylactic biofilm prevention, complementary strategies may be required to clear established biofilms.

title: The structural context of mutations in proteins predicts their effect on antibiotic resistance
abstract: In, a prevalent and deadly pathogen, resistance to antibiotics evolves primarily through non-synonymous mutations in proteins. Sequence-based analyses can uncover the genetic basis of antibiotic resistance, but these methods focus on primary sequence and often neglect other biological signals, such as protein structural information. We hypothesize that integrating the structural context of mutations improves the prediction of effects on function and phenotype. We curate high-confidence structural annotations for theproteome from 1350 crystallography and 2337 AlphaFold predictions, and mutations from over 31,000isolates. We demonstrate that mutations in proteins known to cause resistance are clustered in 3D space, even in proteins where inactivating mutations at any position are thought to cause resistance. We find over 450 proteins in theproteome that display signals of clustered mutations, many of which have a known relationship with antibiotic resistance. We show that a supervised classifier trained on 3D distance to known resistance sites alone has an1 score of 96.5% at classifying mutations as resistance-conferring on a held-out test set. This work demonstrates that protein structure provides useful information for categorizing which variants may cause antibiotic resistance, even when the majority of structures are AI-predicted.

title: The dual action of Mume Fructus against Helicobacter pylori: targeting bacterial viability and virulence
abstract: To tackle the global challenge ofantibiotic resistance, this study screened aqueous extracts from 17 edible plants with reported anti-potential and found Mume Fructus extract (MFE) as a potential food-derived anti-candidate, and subsequently investigated its efficacy and mechanisms. MFE exerted potent and consistent inhibitory activity against both standard and multidrug-resistant (MDR)strains. It alleviated gastric inflammation and restored the mucosal structure in mice, and protected GES-1 cells from-induced damage in a dose-dependent manner. Organic acids were identified as the potential key compounds with enhanced cytoprotective effects. MFE and its organic acids significantly downregulatedvirulence genes, whereas organic acids bound to the CagA oncoprotein. These findings suggest that MFE exerts anti-effects through direct bacterial growth suppression and virulence attenuation. Given its potent anti-MDR strain activity and favorable safety, MFE represents a promising functional food ingredient for the adjunctive dietary management ofinfection.

title: Hospital wastewater-based antimicrobial resistance epidemiology: a scoping review
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) offers pooled biological samples of defined populations, complementing clinical surveillance for infectious diseases. Hospitals are hotspots for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We performed a scoping review assessing hospital wastewater for AMR monitoring. We searched Medline, Embase, Biosis, Web of Science, and biorxiv.org from inception to May 5, 2026, for studies using hospital wastewater to monitor AMR. The primary outcome was AMR detection and concordance with traditional surveillance. Concordance was reported by resistance class, and reported as strain- or gene-level, as discordant, or as not assessed. Secondary outcomes included sampling methods, and laboratory techniques. Of 4,695 screened studies, 36 from 22 countries met inclusion criteria (high-income 53%, upper-middle-income 42%, and lower-middle-income 5%). Traditional surveillance used mostly routine diagnostics (58%); only 39% of studies aligned temporally with wastewater sampling. Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase-producing organisms showed strain-level concordance in 2/6 studies, and gene-level concordance in 4/6; carbapenem resistance showed strain-level concordance in 2/9 and gene-level concordance in 4/9. Concordance was present for vancomycin-resistant enterococci (2/3), while inconsistent for(0/2) and. One study quantified correlation statistically, finding strong association (Spearman's rho = .88). Wastewater sampling methods included grab sampling (39%), composite sampling (36%), and was unreported (25%). Most studies combined culture-based (89%) and molecular methods (PCR 75%, WGS 42%, metagenomics 17%), mostly targeting Gram-negatives (83%). Hospital WBE showed variable concordance with traditional surveillance, but methodological heterogeneity and limited temporal alignment constrain comparisons. Standardized frameworks and patient-level studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, are needed.

title: Biodegradation Characteristics of Piperacillin by Marine Bacillus cereus PP1 and Genome-Guided Mining of Candidate β-Lactamases
abstract: Antibiotic residues in aquatic environments are an increasing concern because they may retain antibacterial activity, promote antibiotic resistance and generate transformation products with uncertain ecological risks. In this study, marine-derived bacteria were screened for their ability to degrade representative β-lactam antibiotics. Strain PP1, identified as Bacillus cereus, was selected for detailed characterization because of its outstanding degradation capacity toward piperacillin, ceftiofur and cephalexin, especially its efficient removal of piperacillin at a high initial concentration of 100 mg/L. During a 48-h incubation, B. cereus PP1 completely degraded piperacillin and reduced the antibacterial activity of the treated solution against representative Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. UHPLC-MS/MS analysis indicated that piperacillin was transformed mainly through β-lactam ring opening, together with side-chain cleavage and downstream fragmentation reactions. The degradation products showed no obvious hemolytic activity under the tested conditions, whereas live PP1 exhibited hemolysis, highlighting the need for biosafety evaluation before live-cell application. Whole-genome sequencing revealed that PP1 contains a single circular chromosome of 5,285,738 bp and has broad metabolic potential. CARD, CAZy and VFDB annotations indicated antibiotic tolerance, hydrolytic enzyme resources and virulence-associated features. Targeted mining using a local β-lactamase database identified two candidate β-lactamase genes, PP1_BLA_A and PP1_BLA_B, assigned to class A and class B β-lactamases, respectively. Structure prediction and molecular docking further suggested that both enzymes can accommodate piperacillin, but with distinct binding modes. These findings indicate that B. cereus PP1 is a valuable source for β-lactamase discovery and enzyme-based β-lactam bioremediation.

title: Ionic liquid/PDMS coated nanostructured ZnO surfaces for superior antibacterial activity
abstract: The development of nanostructured antibacterial surfaces has gained significant attention due to the urgent need to combat bacterial colonization and biofouling across food, healthcare, and marine sectors. Among functional metal oxides, zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures are particularly promising owing to their rich morphology, favourable physicochemical attributes, and intrinsic bactericidal properties. Here, we utilize a green, eco-friendly Hot Water Treatment (HWT) method to fabricate dense ZnO nanorod arrays on zinc substrates. To overcome the practical limitations and challenges of conventional antibacterial coatings, such as poor operational stability, cytotoxicity, and the risk of antimicrobial resistance, we developed a durable hybrid coating composed of an imidazolium-based ionic liquid stabilized with polydimethylsiloxane. The resulting hybrid-coated nanostructured surfaces exhibit superior antibacterial efficacy against Escherichia coli through a combination of topography-induced mechanical strain and membrane disruption.

title: Whole-genome insights into a multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming, and pathogenic Salmonella Umbilo isolate and molecular characterization of rare Salmonella serovars from poultry
abstract: Salmonellosis is one of the leading foodborne zoonoses worldwide, with contaminated poultry products representing a major source of human infection. This study characterized rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks with respect to biofilm formation, virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), CRISPR loci diversity, and genomic features. Salmonella isolates were conventionally isolated from drug swap samples and serotyped. Biofilm- (csgA, csgB, csgD, ompR, adrA, rpoS, and fimH) and virulence-associated genes (sipA, sipD, sopB, sopD, sopE, sopE2, sitC, sifA, ssaR, spvC, and pefA) were investigated. CRISPR loci and phenotypic AMR were examined. The Salmonella isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index, was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Bioinformatic analyses were conducted to determine its plasmid, AMR, and virulence capacity. Thirty rare Salmonella serovars were identified including, Aba, Atento, Ball, Blegdam, Bonariensis, Bradford, Chandans, Fallowfield, Ferruch, Idikan, II (1,9,12:g,m,s,t:e,n,x), Inganda, Korbol, Leeuwarden, Menden, Naestved, Ohlstedt, Papuana, Petahtikve, Sandow, Schwarzengrund, Svedvi, Telaviv, Thompson, Tinda, Tsevie, Tumodi, Umbilo, Uppsala, and Vejle. CsgA-B-C (100.0%) and sipA (96.7%) were the most prevalent genes. S. Sandow harbored all examined genes. CRISPR2 locus (23.3%) was more prevalent than the CRISPR1 locus (3.3%). Resistance to streptomycin (56.7%) and sulfonamides (46.7%) was most common, whereas 40.0% of the isolates were MDR. WGS of the S. Umbilo isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index (0.48), identified the IncHI2A plasmid (a key factor in horizontal transfer of AMR genes), 12 AMR genes (responsible for resistance to beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols, and lincosamides), and 181 virulence-associated genes (involved in adhesion, invasion, chemotaxis, intracellular survival, and environmental persistence). The detection of highly resistant and potentially pathogenic S. Umbilo, previously linked to a multinational foodborne outbreak in Europe, highlights its potential public health significance. MLST further proved useful for serovar prediction, with ST2014. Rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks possess substantial virulence, biofilm-forming, and AMR potential. These findings highlight the importance of including rare serovars in surveillance and control programs to mitigate foodborne transmission and the spread of AMR.

title: Genomic insights into high-sugar tolerance and probiotic properties of Pediococcus pentosaceus MP13, a potential probiotic isolated from traditional fermented rose jam
abstract: Pediococcus pentosaceus MP13 was previously isolated from traditionally fermented rose jam, a high-sugar fermentation environment. This strain exhibits promising fermentation and probiotic-related properties, but the genomic features potentially associated with its tolerance to high-sugar conditions remain unclear. This study evaluated the effects of sugar stress, selected probiotic properties, and characterized genomic features of MP13. Increasing sugar concentrations inhibited MP13 growth and increased extracellular conductivity and nucleic acid leakage, both approaching plateaus at higher concentrations, while cells exposed to 55% sugar retained relatively intact coccoid morphology. MP13 also showed appreciable cell surface hydrophobicity, approximately 75% auto-aggregation, and inhibitory activity against the tested indicator bacteria. Its complete genome comprised a single 1 939 576 bp circular chromosome with a GC content of 38.46%. Comparative genomic analysis showed high overall similarity to related P. pentosaceus strains, while revealing inter-strain genomic variation. MP13 utilized 22 of 49 tested carbohydrates, and genome annotation identified diverse carbohydrate metabolism-related pathways, 212 putative CAZyme genes, and 33 substrate-specific PTS genes, suggesting broad genetic potential for carbohydrate metabolism despite phenotype-genotype discrepancies for sucrose and d-melibiose. Functional annotation identified genes with predicted roles in osmotic, acid, and bile stress responses, and adhesion, while genome mining revealed putative bacteriocin-associated loci. Safety assessment showed a non-hemolytic phenotype and no known toxin or biogenic amine biosynthesis genes, while no corresponding known acquired antimicrobial resistance genes determinants were detected for previously reported resistance to gentamicin, erythromycin, and penicillin. The phenotypic and genomic characteristics of P. pentosaceus MP13 support its further evaluation for sugar-rich food fermentation and as a probiotic candidate. Carbohydrate metabolism- and stress-response-related genomic features suggest potential contributions to high-sugar tolerance, but their functional roles require expression- and function-based validation. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: [Translated article] The "Trojan horse" against antimicrobial resistance: Siderophore conjugates and public health
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance, particularly in carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales such as KPC-type, represents a critical threat to public health in Latin America, associated with high mortality rates and increased healthcare costs. This systematic review aims to evaluate the therapeutic potential of siderophore-drug and siderophore-peptide conjugates against priority multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii, analyzing their efficacy, mechanisms of action, and implementation challenges. A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases up to August 2025. Key terms such as "siderophore conjugates", "Trojan horse antibiotics", "antimicrobial resistance", and "Gram-negative bacteria" were used. Preclinical and clinical studies, reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2019 and 2025 were included, selecting 55 references based on relevance to the topic, currency, and methodological quality. This review is a narrative review with a systematic literature search, developed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Siderophore conjugates, via the "Trojan horse" mechanism, effectively exploit bacterial iron uptake systems to deliver antimicrobial agents in a targeted manner. They overcome key resistance mechanisms such as β-lactamase production, porin alterations, and efflux pump activity, while reducing systemic toxicity and preserving commensal microbiota. Clinical evidence (e.g., cefiderocol) and preclinical studies confirm their efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains, achieving significant reductions in minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). However, critical challenges were identified: optimization of chemical stability and intracellular drug release, complexity in synthesis and industrial scaling under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, and regulatory and logistical barriers in resource-limited settings. Siderophore conjugates offer a targeted therapeutic approach against multidrug-resistant pathogens by exploiting the bacteria's own iron-uptake systems. The available evidence ranges from clinical results with cefiderocol to preclinical developments with other platforms. Their application, however, faces challenges that span chemical optimization, manufacturing, regulation, and access in clinical settings.

Digital health technologies for the prevention and management of urinary tract infections in menopausal women: A systematic review
abstract: Urinary tract infections are among the most common infectious diseases in women, with incidence increasing after menopause. The genitourinary syndrome of menopause increases susceptibility to recurrent urinary tract infections through urogenital atrophy and microbiome disruption, compounding the risk of antimicrobial resistance. To synthesise evidence on digital health technologies for the prevention and management of urinary tract infections in menopausal women. Four databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane) were systematically searched from January 2000 to March 2026 following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Study quality was assessed using risk-of-bias and critical appraisal tools. Menopausal status was classified as explicitly, proxy or not reported. Of 9935 records identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. Four technology clusters emerged: patient-facing digital interventions (n = 4), predictive machine-learning models (n = 7), clinician-facing electronic health record-integrated decision support systems (n = 2), and point-of-care biosensors (n = 1). Digital tools reduced inappropriate antibiotic prescribing by up to 60% and ciprofloxacin use by 80.5%. Predictive models achieved discrimination values of 0.57-0.96 but lacked prospective validation. No study applied formal staging criteria for reproductive aging or integrated hormonal variables. Time to diagnosis and treatment were not assessed. Digital health technologies show potential for antimicrobial stewardship in menopausal women with urinary tract infections but remain largely insensitive to menopause-specific biological factors. One randomised controlled trial demonstrated increased uptake of vaginal oestrogen therapy with the use of these technologies, providing evidence of digitally supported non-antibiotic prevention. Future research should integrate menopausal staging, hormonal variables, and user-centred design. CRD420251052764.

title: Driving factors for the distribution of i/eARGs in livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater across China
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), as emerging pollutants, have become a growing environmental concern owing to their wide distribution, durability, and potential adverse effects on humans, animals and the surrounding environments. Livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater (LPMW), the major reservoir of antibiotics, has higher abundance of extracellular ARGs (eARGs) compared with other environments. This review summarizes the abundance of intracellular ARGs (iARGs) and eARGs in LPMW in China. The absolute abundance of iARGs and eARGs in LPMW were 10-10and 10-10copies/mL or copies/g, respectively, with sul1, sul2, tetQ, tetW, tetG, ermB, ermF, blaand blaas the main detected i/eARGs types. Subsequently, the study summarized the intrinsic molecular and biological properties, extrinsic drivers, and methodological influences that may influence the abundance of i/eARGs. Discrepancies in the absolute abundance of i/eARGs could be due to factors such as genetic location, sample sources, antibiotic residues and manure treatment methods. Besides, the efficiencies of extracellular DNA(eDNA) extraction methods commonly used for LPMW samples were compared and quantitative methods of i/eARGs were evaluated, which could also introduce subjective bias into i/eARGs abundance. Limitations related to the current eDNA extraction methods and quantitative methods, the establishment of the safety thresholds for eARGs, in situ monitoring methods, and the role of phages in the spread of ARGs were discussed as future prospects. This review highlights the importance of environmental risk assessment for i/eARGs, lay theoretical basis for the effective removal of i/eARGs for further researches and provides advice for future governance and regulatory measurement.

title: Unravelling structurally diverse broad-spectrum antimicrobial secondary metabolites isolated from the stem of Tinospora cordifolia
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most critical global health challenges of the 21st century; there is an urgent need to discover and develop novel antimicrobial agents to strengthen the current therapeutic armamentarium. Subsequently, natural products serve as a reservoir of unique and structurally diverse molecules, which offer promising opportunities for discovering and developing novel therapeutics to combat AMR. In our present study, phytochemical investigation of the stems of Tinospora cordifolia, an Ayurvedic medicinal plant, resulted in the isolation of 28 chemical constituents. Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, including 1D, 2D NMR, and HRESI-MS. All isolated compounds were then screened for antibacterial potential against a panel of clinically relevant Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus) and Gram-negative (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli) pathogens. Initial screening at 25 μM concentration revealed three active hits (TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6), which were further evaluated by MIC and MBC determination assays. All three compounds exhibited MIC and MBC values in the range of 0.015 μM to 16 μM and 0.015 μM to 32 μM, respectively. Furthermore, cytotoxicity assessment using murine macrophages (RAW 264.7 and J774A.1) revealed good biocompatibility with a satisfactory selectivity index, while hemolysis assays confirmed very minimal erythrocyte toxicity at the tested concentration. Furthermore, in silico ADME/toxicity analysis using SwissADME and pkCSM predicted favourable pharmacokinetics and drug-likeness properties, although structural optimization may further improve their developability. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6 as valuable candidates for novel antibacterial drug development.
